verses.1: Al-Mizan presents the chapter as Meccan and as a sustained answer to faithless arrogance and false disputation: it recalls former deniers' fate and their Hereafter, proves God's oneness in lordship and divinity, commands the Prophet's steadfast worship, and promises help to him and the faithful. Claims of Medinan verses lack merit. The Book's ‘sending down’ means that it is sent by God. His being All-mighty and All-knowing primarily answers deniers who mistake ignorance for knowledge and pride in it: their arrogance cannot overcome His might, and their false arguments cannot defeat truth sent with absolute knowledge; explanations based only on inimitability or style are less apt. Al-Mizan reads ‘forgiver of sins’ and ‘acceptor of repentance’ as continuous attributes of action. Together they concern sinful servants: God forgives the repentant and may forgive for other reasons, such as intercession. ‘Severe in retribution’ names punishment consequent on sin, while al-ṭawl denotes enduring bounty, more specific than a general bestowal of benefits. These names explain the Book's descent: God knows His creatures' need for a true call, their continual bounties in this life, their division in the Hereafter between felicitous and wretched, and who is ready for forgiveness or deserves punishment. The Book guides toward felicity and organizes worldly life. ‘There is no deity but Him; to Him is the destination’ consequently requires exclusive worship and recalls the Resurrection, whose fear and hope motivate obedience. Al-Mizan says disputing God's signs means using falsehood to invalidate the truth to which they point, not arguing in truth's defence, which the Qur'an commands in the best manner (16:125). The faithless are those in whom disbelief has become entrenched, and their bustle in towns is their progress through worldly health, ease, and blessing; it must not suggest to the Prophet that they have outmanoeuvred God. Noah's people and later factions similarly denied, falsely disputed, and sought to seize their messengers, but God seized and punished them. The shift to the first person emphasizes that no one can intervene against His retribution. Thus the punishment that befell past deniers confirms that God's word has become due against all faithless people, including contemporary deniers, for the Fire; ‘the word of your Lord’ also reassures the Prophet of the strength of his divine support.

verses.4: Al-Mizan says that after establishing the Book's truth through the divine attributes, the verse turns to those who use false arguments to reject the truth indicated by God's signs. Their dispute is not a defence of truth, which the Qur'an permits in the best manner (16:125), but an attempt to invalidate it; they therefore face the punishment for which the Book was also sent. ‘The faithless’ denotes people in whom disbelief is entrenched. Their bustle through towns means their passage through worldly health, comfort, and other blessings, not an escape from God or proof that He is powerless, so it must not grieve or mislead the Prophet.
verses.5: Al-Mizan treats the histories of Noah's people and later factions as an answer to deniers who imagine their arrogant disputation has brought no consequence or has no precedent. Earlier nations denied the signs, used falsehood against truth, and tried to seize, kill, expel, or otherwise harm their messengers; God then punished them. The shift from speaking about God to ‘I seized them’ stresses that their fate rests on God alone and admits no rescuer or intercessor. The question about His retribution recalls the known severity of those historical punishments and warns the present deniers accordingly.
verses.6: Al-Mizan takes ‘that’ to refer to God's seizing and punishing the preceding deniers. As they were punished in this world, God's word has become due against all past faithless people, including the disbelievers among the Prophet's people, for punishment in the Hereafter and the Fire. Restricting the phrase to the Meccan disbelievers lacks contextual support. Calling it ‘the word of your Lord,’ rather than ‘My word,’ reassures the Prophet that his supporting pillar is powerful.
verses.7: Al-Mizan infers that the bearers of the Throne are angels from their conjunction with those around it and from (39:75). They carry the Throne, the locus from which divine commands issue, while the angels around it are the brought-near angels. Their glorification and praise deny every defect and partner while praising God's acts and governance; their faith is belief in His absolute oneness in lordship and divinity, refuting the idolaters' treatment of exalted angels as independent lords. Their prayer asks forgiveness for believers who repent by returning in faith to God and follow His way, Islam, and asks protection from hell. Mercy is the source of every blessing, while knowledge identifies every being ready to receive it, so the angels invoke both before this request.
verses.8: Al-Mizan says the angels repeat ‘Our Lord’ to seek sympathy and ask admission to the promised Gardens of Eden for believers and every forebear, spouse, or descendant worthy of paradise. The promise was conveyed by prophets, messengers, and scriptures. The prayer distinguishes the believers who repent and follow God's way, who are followed, from the worthy relatives who follow them, and is broader than (52:21), which names only descendants and conditions their joining on faith. ‘All-mighty, All-wise’ does not replace mercy with severity: God's comprehensive mercy means limitless power to give or withhold, while His comprehensive knowledge entails that His acts are perfectly ordered. The attributes therefore appeal to the mercy and knowledge invoked at the beginning of the prayer.
verses.9: Al-Mizan understands the angels' request to save ‘them’ as covering both the penitent and the worthy. ‘Evils’ may mean sins with an implicit recompense, but the preferred sense is the terrors and hardships of the Day of Resurrection, not hell's punishment already mentioned. The verse thus indicates that people are requited with their very deeds. From the prayer the commentary derives the etiquette of beginning supplication with praise, then requests, and the relevant Beautiful Names; forgiveness precedes paradise because barriers to a blessing must first be removed. A request for forgiveness does not show that acceptance of repentance is merely optional: God has made its acceptance obligatory upon Himself, yet believers still ask to see His promise fulfilled and express longing for His generosity. What necessarily proceeds from God is still grace, because no outside agent compels Him; it is His own fixed decree and gift.
verses.10: Al-Mizan reads the proclamation as occurring before the faithless enter hell, when they recognize that their earlier refusal of prophetic calls to faith has brought eternal ruin. Their self-hatred is therefore an outrage, but God's outrage at their rejection is greater.
verses.11: Al-Mizan places the confession in hell, after the divine proclamation. The faithless, now certain of resurrection and the return to God, confess their sins and beg for any escape, but too late; forgetting the Hereafter had made them sink into sin. Their two deaths and two lives explain how certainty came: death in this world, life in Barzakh, death there, and life for Resurrection. Worldly life is not counted because it did not produce that certainty. This refutes readings that make the first death pre-ensoulment, omit the resurrection life, appeal to pre-existence, or make ‘two’ a mere idiom for repetition; the verse uses the literal number and its purpose is not to recount every stage of existence. The indefiniteness of ‘any way out’ expresses desperation after every other avenue has failed.
verses.12: Al-Mizan treats the verse as a rebuke on the Day of Resurrection, though it may also warn in this world. The faithless persistently rejected every implication of God's oneness while accepting associationism, neglecting their duties and respect toward Him. They thereby cut themselves off from His mercy, so He judges them without leniency. The declaration that judgment belongs to the All-exalted, All-great is thus a context-specific warning, strengthened by those two names, not only a detached general statement.
verses.13: Al-Mizan takes God's signs as proofs of His exclusive lordship and divinity in the natural world, through messengers, and through revelation. They establish that the deity whose worship brings human flourishing must guide people to that worship; only God has such cosmic signs and prophetic proofs, whereas the idolaters' deities have none. Provision from heaven supplies a further proof, since provision is a function of lordship; it may mean rain or provisions emerging from the Unseen into the visible realm. The commentary reports Imām ʿAlī's formulation that, if the Lord had a partner, that partner's messengers would also have come. Only one who returns penitently takes this admonition, for obstinate disbelief disables a person from learning from proofs or following truth.
verses.14: Al-Mizan reads the command as addressed to all capable of following the preceding proofs, rather than to the obstinate faithless who deny and dispute through falsehood. Since the signs establish God's oneness and He alone provides, people must supplicate Him and devote religion exclusively to Him. The deniers who abhor divine unity have no remaining hope in signs or proofs; worshippers should remain devoted even if such people detest it.
verses.15: Al-Mizan reads the three descriptions as predicates of the One who shows His signs and as part of the warning that follows. Raiser of ranks and Lord of the Throne point to the exalted, veiled dominion from which commands descend through lofty ranks, perhaps the angels' heavens; on the Day of Meeting the veil will be removed and all will see that sovereignty and judgment belong only to Him. He casts the Spirit of His command, the Spirit of (17:85), down with the angels of revelation upon the prophets and messengers He chooses, so that they may warn. The Day of Meeting can name several convergences, but the meeting of Creator and creation is supported by Qur'anic descriptions of meeting the Lord: all distractions are severed, God appears as the Manifest Truth, and people emerge from graves toward Him.
verses.16: Al-Mizan explains the Day of Meeting as the removal of every imagined bond and veil that concealed God's all-encompassing sovereignty, exclusive lordship, and judgment. Nothing inward or outward, remembered or forgotten, remains hidden from Him. God's own question and answer, ‘To whom does sovereignty belong today? To Allah, the One, the All-dominant,’ disclose that reality. He alone has sovereignty because domination deprives things of independent authority, and His oneness makes that authority exclusively His.
verses.17: Al-Mizan says the Day's significance is that every soul is requited with its own deeds. There can be no injustice through error because God's swift reckoning means that judging one soul never distracts Him from another. Deliberate injustice is also impossible here, since recompense is the very deeds each soul earned.
verses.18: Al-Mizan explains hearts at throats as an image of extreme fear, as though the heart has leapt to the epiglottis, and kāẓimīn as suppressed, intense grief. The warning adds that wrongdoers will have neither a sympathetic close associate able to aid them nor an intercessor whose plea is heard.
verses.19: Al-Mizan takes ‘the treachery of the eyes’ to mean concealed sins of sight, such as a stolen glance, rather than every eye-sin indiscriminately; its pairing with what breasts hide displays God's complete knowledge. What the breasts conceal includes inward disbelief, hypocrisy, and sinful thoughts. The alternative grammatical reading, ‘treacherous eyes,’ is less fitting.
verses.20: Al-Mizan makes this a further proof of God's exclusive divinity. A deity must judge servants and judge between them; God alone does so on the Day of Resurrection, while the invoked associates are themselves His servants without sovereignty. His judgment also includes His creative decree over particular affairs and His promulgation of religion as the way to Him, so none who lacks a share in creation has a share in judgment. As All-hearing and All-seeing, God possesses knowledge of every object of hearing and sight through His own essence; others possess such faculties only by His endowment and permission.
verses.21: Al-Mizan reads the verse as a rebuke: the disbelievers should travel, observe the destroyed nations that denied their messengers, and take warning. Those peoples surpassed them in power and in the remains they left—fortified cities, strongholds, and lofty palaces—yet Allah seized them for their sins. A wāqin, a defender from wiqāya, could not protect them from His punishment.
verses.22: Al-Mizan explains that the punishment followed the peoples’ defiance of their messengers’ bayyināt, manifest proofs. Allah’s seizure therefore displays His strength and severity in retribution.
verses.23: Al-Mizan takes Moses’ āyāt to be miracles such as the staff becoming a serpent and the shining hand, and sulṭān mubīn to be the divine power supporting them, which prevented Pharaoh from killing Moses and extinguishing his guidance. It notes the alternative allocation of proofs to āyāt and miracles to the manifest authority. Pharaoh, Haman, and Korah are singled out as the leading sources of corruption among Egyptians and Israelites.
verses.24: Al-Mizan takes Moses’ āyāt to be miracles such as the staff becoming a serpent and the shining hand, and sulṭān mubīn to be the divine power supporting them, which prevented Pharaoh from killing Moses and extinguishing his guidance. It notes the alternative allocation of proofs to āyāt and miracles to the manifest authority. verses.25: Al-Mizan contrasts Moses’ God-given truth with the plot to kill the sons and spare the women of those who believed with him; Allah made the faithless scheme fail, so they could not harm them. It considers Korah a likely speaker: unlike Pharaoh’s earlier order against all Israelites, this one concerns Moses’ followers, and Korah’s hostility could have aligned his interest with Pharaoh and Haman. Calling them “the faithful who are with him” shows that they supported Moses’ mission.
verses.26: Al-Mizan understands Pharaoh to address elites who had advised leaving Moses alive. His challenge that Moses invoke “his Lord” is insolent mockery of divine rescue. Pharaoh presents killing Moses as protection of religion and public order: Moses would replace their idolatry with worship of the One God and, by gathering followers, might cause rebellion, violence, and insecurity.
verses.27: Al-Mizan contrasts Moses’ appeal for the protection of “my Lord and your Lord” with Pharaoh’s reference to God as Moses’ Lord alone. “Your Lord” consequently means Pharaoh and his people, affirming that God’s authority extends over them and that His protection from their evil is effective. The arrogant unbelievers in the Day of Reckoning include Pharaoh and all who share those traits; no one is safe from such a character.
verses.28: Al-Mizan holds that min āl Firʿawn describes the believer himself, while yaktum īmānahu is a second description: he was an Egyptian of Pharaoh’s family who concealed faith in Moses. It rejects the alternative that he concealed his faith from Pharaoh’s clan, since neither context nor word order supports it, and his repeated “O my people” (yā qawmi) confirms his membership. He rebukes the proposed killing of one who brought bayyināt from their own Lord; his conditional language is conciliatory, not doubt in Moses. If Moses lies, the lie harms him; if true, they face at least some promised punishment, and their profligacy, denial of their Lord, and taking of other lords leave no divine guidance. Al-Mizan therefore rejects treating the final clause as a joint justification of both earlier statements.
verses.29: Al-Mizan reads the believer’s question as a persuasive rebuke: Egypt’s present sovereignty and domination over the Israelites cannot save “us” from Allah’s punishment. By including himself, he makes clear that his counsel seeks their safety as well as his own. Pharaoh’s claim to show only what he sees as advisable and to guide only to rectitude is feigned certainty, presented as objective reality to his people.
verses.30: Al-Mizan identifies the speaker as the believer from Pharaoh’s clan, not Moses. He fears for his people the daʾb—precedent or habitual fate—of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, and later nations, destroyed for continuing disbelief and denial of messengers. Their requital does not imply that Allah wills wrong for His servants.
verses.31: Al-Mizan identifies the speaker as the believer from Pharaoh’s clan, not Moses. verses.32: Al-Mizan explains the Day of Mutual Calls as the Resurrection, perhaps because wrongdoers call each other for aid and in grief. “Turning back” may describe attempts to flee Hell’s punishment before being returned to it, as in (22:22). They will have no protector from Allah: were there one it would be God, but He leaves astray those whom He leaves without a guide.

verses.34: Al-Mizan presents Joseph’s case to illustrate that one whom Allah leaves astray has no guide. The Egyptians remained doubtful of Joseph’s manifest proofs while he lived, then contradicted themselves after his death by claiming Allah would send no messenger after him. This exemplifies Allah’s leading astray the profligate and sceptical.
verses.35: Al-Mizan describes the disputers as doubtful sinners who, having overstepped truth through whim and entrenched scepticism, cannot settle upon knowledge or conviction about guiding proofs. They contest Allah’s signs without authority because the signs oppose their desires. Allah’s sealing of every arrogant tyrant’s heart means that it can neither comprehend proof nor understand argument.
verses.36: Al-Mizan explains Pharaoh’s order to Haman as a demand for a visible sarḥ, a lofty structure, from which to reach the asbāb, means of access, of the heavens and look for Moses’ God. It may have been issued during the believer’s speech after Pharaoh temporarily abandoned killing Moses. Pharaoh either pretended for his people or spoke ignorantly; the commentary regards the observatory reading as good but says neither account coheres with idolatry. Satan made his evil conduct seem fair and diverted him from sound judgment, so his schemes against truth ended in complete ruin.

Satan made his evil conduct seem fair and diverted him from sound judgment, so his schemes against truth ended in complete ruin.
verses.38: Al-Mizan says that following the believer is in reality following Moses. Sabīl al-rashād is the path to truth and everlasting felicity, and guidance is showing that path. The believer’s claim to guide to it deliberately parallels Pharaoh’s earlier claim in (40:29).
verses.39: Al-Mizan makes the world’s being only provision and the Hereafter the abiding home the basis for following the way of rectitude and the religion of truth. Human beings have an eternal life ahead; this world is provision for that journey, which is why the believer next addresses evil and righteous deeds.
verses.40: Al-Mizan reads worldly life as the abode of deeds and the next as the abode of recompense: evil is repaid only by the harm it carries, while righteous believers, male and female alike, enter Paradise and receive provision without reckoning. The equality of men and women is expressly qualified by faith, since good deeds without it are void, as (5:5) indicates. The verse thus states the religion’s concise call to act virtuously in view of eternal recompense, adding the unreckoned provision of the righteous.
verses.41: Al-Mizan says the believer of Pharaoh’s clan marvels that he calls his people to salvation from the Fire while they, whether directly or through their actions, call him to idolatry and so to the Fire. The terms name outcomes for their respective deeds. They ask him to associate partners without knowledge or evidence; he calls them to the All-mighty, who cannot be overcome, and the All-forgiver, who forgives those who repent and believe, that they may submit to Him.
verses.42: Al-Mizan says the believer of Pharaoh’s clan marvels that he calls his people to salvation from the Fire while they, whether directly or through their actions, call him to idolatry and so to the Fire. The terms name outcomes for their respective deeds. They ask him to associate partners without knowledge or evidence; he calls them to the All-mighty, who cannot be overcome, and the All-forgiver, who forgives those who repent and believe, that they may submit to Him.
verses.43: Al-Mizan argues that the alleged partners have no true call in this world or the Hereafter: they send no messengers and none returns to them. Allah alone summons through prophets and proofs now, and all creation will return to Him for judgment, as (17:52) says. Since rubūbiyya necessarily entails a daʿwa in both worlds, only Allah is the real God; those who cross the bounds of servanthood are inmates of the Fire.
verses.44: Al-Mizan takes the believer’s warning as a threat that his people will remember his counsel when they behold punishment. His tafwīḍ, entrusting his affair to Allah, returns to God even the part he seems to possess and leaves him withdrawn from deciding it. It differs from tawakkul, making God one’s wakīl and relying on Him, and taslīm, total submission to His will; these stations of ʿubūdiyya rise from tawakkul through tafwīḍ to taslīm. Allah’s seeing servants explains the entrustment, and the explicit name stresses that He sees because He is Allah.
verses.45: Al-Mizan says Allah saved the believer from Pharaoh’s supporters’ schemes, while their clan was besieged by the terrible punishment of Fire. It distinguishes their exposure to it before the Hour from their later entry into it: the first is punishment in Barzakh, the world between death and resurrection, and the second is more severe. Both are the same Hereafter Fire, but those in Barzakh suffer it from afar whereas its later inmates are put within it. Exposure morning and evening signifies continual punishment and perhaps their still incomplete detachment from worldly time.

verses.47: Al-Mizan confines this argument in the Fire to Pharaoh’s clan, rejecting readings that make it all unbelievers or the Quraysh. Their weak members ask their arrogant leaders for even a share of relief because their worldly habit of relying on leaders persists despite knowing that no soul can avail another on that day. The leaders answer that all are in the Fire: it is the Day of recompense, and Allah’s judgment has annulled every imagined power, influence, and recourse, leaving them equal in punishment.
verses.48: Al-Mizan confines this argument in the Fire to Pharaoh’s clan, rejecting readings that make it all unbelievers or the Quraysh. The leaders answer that all are in the Fire: it is the Day of recompense, and Allah’s judgment has annulled every imagined power, influence, and recourse, leaving them equal in punishment.
verses.49: Al-Mizan begins a dialogue between the inmates of the Fire, including Pharaoh’s clan, and Hell’s keepers. Having lost hope that Allah will answer them directly, they ask the angels to seek only a reduction of one day’s punishment. The day is measured by their present world, so the request is for relief from a portion of the punishment.
verses.50: Al-Mizan says Hell’s guardians make the inmates admit that messengers brought manifest proofs; that admission amounts to knowingly denying prophethood (nubuwwa). Telling them to supplicate for themselves implies that their pleas for relief from what they denied will not be answered; the final statement is apparently the angels’ speech, though it may be Allah’s. Genuine supplication requires earnest dependence on Allah alone, but their worldly denial remains a punished moral burden even after certainty comes in the Hereafter. The passage rejects the claim that no supplication by a disbeliever is ever answered: it concerns what they had denied, while other verses affirm answers to all people in need.
verses.51: Al-Mizan promises divine help to messengers and believers as classes, not help to every individual messenger in every circumstance. It refers to its earlier explanation of al-naṣr al-ilāhī, divine assistance.
verses.52: Al-Mizan identifies this as the day when witnesses rise. The wrongdoers’ excuses are certain to be offered, and verses saying they will not speak or be allowed excuses, such as (77:35–6), concern a particular stage or fate within the Resurrection rather than the whole day. Their curse means distance from Allah’s mercy, and the ills of the abode mean Hell.
verses.53: Al-Mizan concludes the account of Moses, Pharaoh, and the believer by affirming the truth of Moses’ guidance and the wickedness of the response to it. Hudā is the religion sent with Moses, and the Children of Israel inherited the Torah in the sense that it remained among them for practice and guidance. The Book guides all, while serving as an admonition especially for those endowed with intellect.
verses.54: Al-Mizan concludes the account of Moses, Pharaoh, and the believer by affirming the truth of Moses’ guidance and the wickedness of the response to it. Hudā is the religion sent with Moses, and the Children of Israel inherited the Torah in the sense that it remained among them for practice and guidance. The Book guides all, while serving as an admonition especially for those endowed with intellect.
verses.55: Al-Mizan concludes from the prior account that the Prophet must endure the idolaters’ persecution and false disputation, certain that Allah will fulfill His promise to help truth and its people. Seeking forgiveness for his sin means a sin relative to him, not disobedience to Allah in view of his infallibility; a reported alternative takes it as intercession (shafāʿa) for his umma. Praising Allah morning and evening may mean continuous praise or those times specifically. Some identify it with the subḥ and ʿaṣr prayers and call the verse Medinan, but the Night Journey narrations establish the five daily prayers in Mecca before the Emigration; if it names two obligatory prayers, it would be Meccan before that institution.
verses.56: Al-Mizan reassures the Prophet that disputers of Allah’s signs act from vanity, not truth-seeking, genuine doubt, proof, or authority. Their aim is to invalidate and extinguish truth, but pride can never attain that aim. He is therefore commanded to seek Allah’s protection from them and their vanity; the All-hearing hears servants’ supplications and the All-seeing knows their needs and hardship.
verses.57: Al-Mizan argues that those who dispute Allah’s signs cannot thwart His plan: the Creator who was not hindered by the vastness of the heavens and earth cannot be overcome by human beings, a minute part of that creation. Most people are ignorant enough to imagine that vain dispute and scheming can defeat Him.
verses.58: Al-Mizan contrasts the seer with the blind as the faithful who do righteous deeds with evildoers whose hearts Allah has made blind to admonition. The switch from speaking of “them” to addressing “you” makes the final statement a direct rebuke for taking little admonition.
verses.59: Al-Mizan says the certain coming of the Hour, despite most people’s disbelief, precedes Allah’s summons to call on and worship Him. It recalls the believer from Pharaoh’s clan, who likewise stressed the imminent Hour, Allah’s call in this world and the next, and the absence of such a call from idols.
verses.60: Al-Mizan presents this as Allah’s universal summons to His servants and His unrestricted promise to answer their prayers, not confined to a group or dependent on conditions. By calling supplication duʿāʾ and then describing disdain for it as disdain for worship (ʿibāda), the verse shows that supplicating to Allah is worship. Those who disdain it enter Hell humiliated.
verses.61: Al-Mizan says Allah made the dark night for rest from daytime labor and the bright day for seeking provision; together they are pillars of ordered human existence. Attributing visibility to day is figurative abstraction, not hyperbole. The verse recalls Allah’s generosity and rebukes human failure to thank Him through worship, using “people” to mark ingratitude as an ingrained human trait.
verses.62: Al-Mizan identifies Allah as Lord because He orders human affairs through night and day, and as Creator and therefore Lord of all things: khalq cannot be separated from tadbīr. No other lord can exist, and because ulūhiyya follows from rubūbiyya, none besides Him is worthy of worship. The verse rebukes those who nevertheless turn to other worship.
verses.63: Al-Mizan explains that those accustomed to impugning Allah’s signs are led astray because the signs are manifest. Only wilful denial prevents a person from seeing what they indicate.
verses.64: Al-Mizan presents earth as humanity’s dwelling and the sky as its canopy, then points to the perfected human form, its distinctive capacities, and provisions suited to varied appetites. Allah’s governance of human life reveals the single cosmic order by which He alone governs every world. Thus all abundant good has one source: Allah, Lord of all the worlds.
verses.65: Al-Mizan says Allah alone possesses pure, everlasting life in Himself, while every other living thing depends on another for life. Only the inherently living can be inherently worthy of worship; therefore there is no Allah except Him. The command to supplicate requires exclusive faith in Him, and the concluding praise returns to His lordship over all worlds.
verses.66: Al-Mizan says the verse tells the idolaters to abandon hope of persuading the Prophet to worship their idols: manifest proofs from his Lord forbid it, and he is commanded to submit to the Lord of all worlds. Comparing its parallel in Sūrah al-Zumar suggests that this chapter was revealed later.
verses.67: Al-Mizan traces human creation through Adam’s dust—or, alternatively, the terrestrial elements of the drop of fluid—then the clinging mass, birth as infants, developed maturity, old age, and earlier death for some. The specified term is the unalterable final limit of worldly life, distinguished from the preceding stages and affirmed in (6:2). Maturity fulfills material worldly development, whereas applying reason to discern truth is the ultimate purpose of humanity’s spiritual existence.
verses.68: Al-Mizan explains that Allah gives life and death by moving the living from one world to another, both realms in which He disposes blessings for those He governs. His decision is accomplished by the command “Be!” and it is.
verses.69: Al-Mizan takes “Have you not regarded?” as amazement at how disputers of Allah’s signs are led from truth and guidance to falsehood and error, and at the outcome awaiting them. This is not repetition of (40:56): that verse exposed their vanity and failure, whereas this one highlights their misguidance and fate. It rejects explanations that divide the references into separate debates or groups as neglecting the chapter’s overarching purpose.
verses.70: Al-Mizan identifies the Book as the Qur’an and what came with the messengers as the scriptures and teachings whose denial by idolaters is denial of prophethood itself. They will know the reality of their deeds when collars and chains humiliate them, drag them through scalding water, and cast them into the Fire. The future event is made certain by the use of idh. A reported interpretation understands their being cast into the Fire as becoming its fuel, supported by (2:24) and (21:98).

verses.73: Al-Mizan says the condemned will be asked why the partners they associated with Allah do not help or intercede. Their answer that the partners have forsaken them may mean that their gods were only empty names and false ideas, so they had invoked nothing real; alternatively, it may be a lie like their denial of polytheism in (6:23). Allah’s leading astray the faithless follows their own concealment of truth: they pursue falsehood as though real, only to find a mirage. On the lying reading, their deeds force a useless lie even when they know it cannot help.

verses.75: Al-Mizan makes the Hereafter’s punishment the result of rejoicing in transient worldly pleasures, attachment to appearances, and delight in the revival of falsehood and erasure of truth. Faraḥ is happiness, whereas maraḥ is its excessive form and is blameworthy. As Majmaʿ al-bayān reports, faraḥ is qualified here as wrongful because it can be praiseworthy or blameworthy, while maraḥ is blameworthy by definition.
verses.76: Al-Mizan explains the command as entry through the assigned gates of Hell and eternal residence there. Its gates (abwāb) denote its different levels (darajāt), and it is the evil resting place of those arrogant toward truth.
verses.77: Al-Mizan draws the command to patience from the fate of those who dispute Allah’s signs: His promise is true. Whether the Prophet sees part of their promised worldly punishment or dies before seeing it, they will return to Allah and cannot escape the fulfillment of His promise.
verses.78: Al-Mizan explains divine help as Allah’s established sunna in judging between messengers and their peoples and making truth prevail, as (10:47) states. No messenger brings a sign by independent power; though the phrase is broader than evidentiary miracles, this context concerns Allah’s judgment between a messenger and people. Allah may permit the Prophet to call down their punishment in his lifetime or take him before it, but when His edict comes judgment is just, falsehood disappears, and falsifiers lose in this world and eternally. The verse may indicate unmentioned messengers, though its Meccan setting may instead mean stories not yet revealed; (4:164) later expressly speaks of messengers not recounted. Majmaʿ al-Bayān reports from ʿAlī that Allah sent an African prophet whose story was not recounted to us.
verses.79: Al-Mizan says Allah calls attention to cattle as provisions made or placed at human disposal: some are ridden and some eaten. Their uses include products such as milk, wool, fur, hair, and hide; riding answers needs such as travel, while cattle and ships carry people across land and sea.

verses.81: Al-Mizan says the mention of Allah’s manifest, visible signs prepares the rebuke that follows. Denying them is thereby a denial of Allah’s oneness.
verses.82: Al-Mizan distinguishes this rebuke from (40:21): that earlier verse warned that Allah would seize rejecters of messengers for sin, whereas this one says that worldly earnings, vaunted knowledge and power, repentance, and regret cannot avail when punishment descends. Fa signals a shift from directly blaming “you” to speaking of “them,” as though Allah turns from the idolaters to His Prophet after their denial of clear signs. The remains of nations stronger in number and quality should show that their worldly achievements could not resist Allah.
verses.83: Al-Mizan reads all the plural pronouns as the nations before the Prophet’s people. Their ʿilm is worldly preoccupation and political expertise, the limited outward knowledge described in (30:7) and (53:29–30); pride in it distracted them from the messengers’ wisdom until the truth they mocked surrounded them. It rejects readings that make this “knowledge” merely derided false belief, Greek or Dahriyyūn philosophy, ignorance called knowledge, mockery of the messengers’ knowledge, or the messengers’ own rejoicing: each lacks textual evidence, conflicts with the cited nations or context, or confuses pronoun referents and faraḥ with mockery. The passage concerns faithless people confronted with manifest proof before punishment, not messengers rejoicing in true knowledge.
verses.84: Al-Mizan explains baʾs as the severity of divine punishment. The condemned profess belief in Allah alone only when they behold that might.
verses.85: Al-Mizan says their faith cannot benefit them once punishment is seen because it is no longer voluntary. By Allah’s settled precedent among His servants, repentance is not accepted after that sighting, and the faithless are therefore losers.
